new_statements.quote: Dans un mot polysyllabique prononcé isolément, il y a toujours une syllabe qui est mise en valeur par un accent expiratoire, relativement faible et souvent difficile à saisir. [...] L'accent a en tout cas un rendement fonctionnel très modeste. [...] Rien ne laisse prédire la place de l'accent dans un mot donné, toutes les syllabes peuvent porter l'accent. La situation se complique du fait que dans le procès morphologique l'accent d'une forme peut se déplacer. Certains monosyllabes gardent ainsi un accent fixe sur la syllabe radicale dans la forme définie, d'autres le reportent sur l'article (ou sur les préfixes possessifs ou démonstratifs).
new_statements.translation: In a polysyllabic word pronounced in isolation there is always one syllable set off by an expiratory accent, relatively weak and often hard to perceive. [...] The accent in any case has a very modest functional yield. [...] Nothing allows one to predict the place of the accent in a given word; all syllables can bear the accent. The situation is complicated by the fact that in morphological processes the accent of a form may move. Some monosyllables thus keep a fixed accent on the root syllable in the definite form, others throw it back onto the article (or onto the possessive or demonstrative prefixes).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ubykh has a weak dynamic word stress, one per polysyllabic word in isolation, whose position is not predictable from phonological shape: any syllable may carry it, and it is lexically specified, with a small number of stress minimal pairs (asán 'it rots' vs ásan 'he sells it', etc.). Stress interacts with morphology: nouns split into a fixed-accent class (stress stays on the root when the definite article a- or possessive/demonstrative prefixes are added: bza 'language', def. abzá) and a mobile class (stress retracts onto the prefix: bža 'tongue', def. ábža; k'ʲabˤə́ 'wolf', def. ák'ʲab(ə)); fixed-accent items are about twice as numerous; the same opposition recurs in verb roots under causativisation. Dybo (1977: 43-44; 1989: 40-41) reanalyses exactly these facts as an Abkhaz-type dominant/recessive morpheme-valency system (stress at the end of the first string of dominant morphemes). Earlier first-hand authors concur that placement is free: Dirr 1928: 8 'Die Betonung scheint frei zu sein'; Mészáros 1934: 40-41 stress is meaning-distinguishing, article stressed in nominalised adjectives vs final stress in predicates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Vogt: in connected speech words form accent groups under a single stress, some words losing their isolation stress (procliticisation), and 'un faible accent secondaire' appears within such groups (p. 32); he regards Mészáros's systematic marking of Nebenbetonung as unmotivated (p. 31). No word-internal secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Very low functional load; informants barely react to misplaced stress; notations of stress vary from text to text and author to author; a few disyllables stressed on the final move stress to their own first syllable rather than to the article (łapqə́ 'race', def. ałápq; nak'ʲə́ 'nail', def. anák'ʲ); unresolved divergent notations (aqáš 'the village' but aqašʁá 'in the village'); stressed syllables carry higher pitch except phrase-finally, where expiratory stress and pitch can disagree.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the word pronounced in isolation (citation forms from Tevfik Esenç); Vogt separately describes phrase-level accent groups in connected texts where isolated-word stresses can be lost. Stress is marked throughout the dictionary entries.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single Ubykh language (ubyk1235, ISO uby) as spoken by the émigré community in Turkey (Manyas district: Hacı Osman köyü etc.); Vogt's data are from the last fluent speaker Tevfik Esenç (1963), Mészáros calls the language 'Päkhy' (self-designation tʷaχə), Dirr's informant was from the Sapanca area. No dialect split relevant to stress is reported; glottocode ubyk1235 applies throughout.

sources.note: pp. 31-33: reviews Dirr/Dumézil/Mészáros disagreement; own conclusion: every polysyllable in isolation has one weakly stressed syllable; a few minimal pairs but very low functional load; 'Rien ne laisse prédire la place de l'accent dans un mot donné, toutes les syllabes peuvent porter l'accent'; stress may move under morphology (fixed-accent vs mobile-accent nouns, article attracts stress in the latter; fixed type about twice as common); accent groups and weak secondary accent in connected speech; stressed syllables higher-pitched except phrase-finally.

sources.note: Second-hand: 'In Dybo (1977) Ubykh was argued to follow Dybo's Rule for stress assignment just like Abkhaz'; reproduces Dybo 1977: 44 Ubykh forms.

sources.citation: Borise, Lena. 2020. Word stress in the languages of the Caucasus. Ms./chapter draft, lingbuzz/004203.
sources.note: Second-hand survey: Dybo's Law analysis extends to Ubykh (examples sɨ-psɐ́ vs sɨ́-nɜ); but sources convey uncertainty about Ubykh stress placement (Dirr 1928: 8; Dumézil 1931: 12); definite ɐ- stress-attracting vs predicative ɐ- not (Mészáros 1934: 41; Vogt 1963: 33; Charachidzé 1989: 368); disyllabic roots fluctuate (Fenwick 2011: 31); causatives shift stress (Charachidzé 1989: 368, 411).

sources.note: pp. 40-41 (scanned, PDF p.22): repeats and slightly expands the 1977 Ubykh material (Table 3): Ubykh has a system 'principially identical' to Abkhaz with two primary nominal accent types and the same contour rule; Ubykh verb shows Abkhaz-like accentuation; complex valency distribution of pronominal prefixes.

sources.note: pp. 43-44 (scanned): for Abkhaz, morphemes carry (+)/(−) accentual valency and 'ударение всегда ставится в конце первой последовательности морфем высшей валентности'; 'Принципиально идентичная система с теми же двумя первичными акцентными типами имени... существует в убыхском', with a table of Ubykh noun forms (a-psá 'fish' type I vs s-ná 'mother' type II) and verb forms; Abkhaz and Ubykh systems genetically related.
